Sampling and representativeness

Who answered, who did not, and what that does to the conclusion

1. Two decisions, two surveys, two wrong answers

On 29 September 2026, in Jaipur, Chhavi Suryavanshi had a one-page memo and two days before her board met. She ran product at Chashma Vision Network, an eyewear retailer with 310 stores and an app serving 11,20,000 customers who had bought in the previous twelve months. The proposal was a home service: an optometrist visits, tests eyes and leaves a frame from a selected range, for ₹1,799. Running it for a year — 140 optometrists, kits, logistics — would cost ₹6.40 crore.

The survey behind the memo ran from 4 to 13 September. Chetana Kulgod, who led research from Chashma's analytics office in Kochi, had invited 28,000 customers at random; 2,058 of 28,000 answered, a response rate of 7.35 per cent; and 651 of 2,058 said they would definitely buy, which is 31.6 per cent. Multiplied against the base and discounted for the gap between saying and doing, that cleared ₹6.40 crore. She had seen such a number in February; it had cost her a pilot.

A week later, on 6 October in Chennai, Elango Raghavendra faced a similar page and a different trap. Ekaagra Shopfloor Systems sold production-tracking software to discrete-manufacturing groups — auto components, pumps, switchgear — with 214 customer groups and ₹60.60 crore of annual recurring revenue. The proposal was a predictive-maintenance module priced as an 18 per cent uplift on each existing contract, against a build-and-run cost of ₹3.60 crore a year. His team had written to the plant manager at every account between 24 August and 11 September; 78 of 214 accounts replied, or 36.4 per cent, and 23 of 78 would pay the uplift: 29.5 per cent.

Raghavendra's response rate was five times Suryavanshi's and his sample was almost a census. Both headlines were nonetheless wrong, for unrelated reasons: her sample was skewed on a variable that mattered, while his was barely skewed and his error was never saying what quantity he was estimating. Only the first is a sampling failure in the textbook sense.

2. The idea, and the quarrel inside it

A population is the set of units a decision concerns; a sample is the subset observed. The sample is representative with respect to a particular quantity — an estimand — when it supports an estimate of that quantity with known, tolerable error. Representativeness is therefore a property of a sample-plus-estimand-plus-estimator, never of a sample alone. William Kruskal and Frederick Mosteller, surveying the literature in 1979 and 1980, found at least six incompatible meanings of "representative sample" and judged the term best avoided without a stated referent.

The machinery exists because censuses are slow and dear. Anders Kiaer argued for purposive selection in the 1890s; Jerzy Neyman's 1934 paper replaced judgement with randomisation, showing that known selection probabilities yield a confidence interval without trusting the selector. P. C. Mahalanobis's Indian Statistical Institute built the National Sample Survey from 1950 on interpenetrating sub-samples that measured field error rather than assuming it away. The Literary Digest poll of 1936 — 2.4 million replies, the wrong president — remains the demonstration that size is not representativeness.

Three schools disagree, live rather than historically. The design-based school, from Neyman through Morris Hansen and Leslie Kish, will sign that only known selection probabilities license an interval estimate, and will not sign that a large sample with rich covariates substitutes for one. The model-based school, from Richard Royall through Roderick Little and Andrew Gelman, will sign that all inference rests on a model and randomisation merely makes a simple one defensible; it will not sign that a 7.35 per cent response rate makes Chashma's survey worthless, since its deficiencies are correctable so far as they are observable. The purposive school will sign that chosen extreme cases are the fastest route to a mechanism, and will not sign that any sample size licenses a claim about how many.

"Name the quantity, then ask whether these units can estimate it, and with what error." Chashma had a sample and no stated error; Ekaagra had an error and no stated quantity.

3. Mechanics: four steps, three of them usually implicit

Experts separate four things that teams fuse into "we ran a survey". Coverage is the frame — the list units can be drawn from. Selection is the draw. Response is which drawn units answer. Estimation turns respondents into a population statement. Randomisation disciplines only the second; the first and third lose the money, and the fourth can sometimes recover it.

Chashma's frame was its transacting-customer table, which excludes anyone buying at a dealer counter without leaving a phone number. Its draw was clean: a 2.5 per cent random slice of each city-tier stratum. Its response was not. Table 1 splits the fieldwork by city tier, a variable on the frame for every customer and plausibly related both to answering a prompt and to wanting an optometrist at home.

Tier 1 is 30.0 per cent of the base and 51.0 per cent of respondents; Tier 3 is 30.0 per cent of the base and 16.3 per cent of respondents. They also differ sharply in interest, 42.0 against 12.5 per cent, which is the condition under which a skewed mix distorts the answer. Post-stratification repairs what is observable: apply each tier's interest rate to its true population, not to its respondent count. Tier 1 gives 0.420 × 3,36,000 = 1,41,120; Tier 2 gives 0.250 × 4,48,000 = 1,12,000; Tier 3 gives 0.125 × 3,36,000 = 42,000. The sum is 2,95,120, which is 26.35 per cent of 11,20,000 — 5.28 percentage points below the pooled 31.63 per cent.

The skipped step is second-order: weighting trades bias for variance, and the trade is quantifiable. Each respondent's weight is the ratio of population share to respondent share: 0.30 / 0.5102 = 0.588 for Tier 1, 0.40 / 0.3265 = 1.225 for Tier 2, 0.30 / 0.1633 = 1.8375 for Tier 3. Kish's design effect is n × Σw² / (Σw)². The weights sum to 2,058 by construction and their squares to 2,505.92, so the design effect is 2,058 × 2,505.92 / 2,058² = 1.218 and the effective sample size is 2,058 / 1.218 = 1,690. Weighting cost 368 interviews of precision, about 18 per cent of the fieldwork, to remove 5.28 points of bias — an excellent trade, but one to price rather than ignore.

The interval follows from the effective size. With a weighted proportion of 0.2635 and 1,690 effective observations, the standard error is √(0.2635 × 0.7365 / 1,690) = 1.07 percentage points, so the 95 per cent interval is 26.35 ± 2.10, or 24.25 to 28.45 per cent. The nominal 2,058 would have given ±1.90 points and false resolution.

Intent must then be converted to behaviour. Chashma's three previous launches turned "definitely buy" into purchase within ninety days at 0.28, 0.31 and 0.31, a simple mean of 0.30. At that ratio the weighted estimate implies 2,95,120 × 0.30 = 88,536 buyers, ₹15.93 crore of revenue at ₹1,799, and at the bundle's 38 per cent gross margin a contribution of ₹6.05 crore — ₹0.35 crore short of the ₹6.40 crore programme cost. The pooled estimate implies 3,54,286 definite buyers, 1,06,286 purchasers, ₹19.12 crore of revenue and ₹7.27 crore of contribution, clearing the hurdle by ₹0.87 crore. Break-even needs ₹6,40,00,000 / (0.38 × ₹1,799) = 93,619 buyers, hence 3,12,064 definite buyers, hence a stated-interest share of 27.86 per cent — a number sitting inside the confidence interval.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

Three conditions, as testable claims. The estimand names a unit. Chashma passes — it wants a count of customers; Ekaagra fails, and that is its whole problem. The variables driving response are on the frame. Chashma passes on city tier and fails on anything attitudinal; Ekaagra passes richly, knowing every account's revenue, plant count and support history. Response and answer are conditionally independent within cells. Neither can test this; both can bound it.

Ekaagra's survey makes the first condition vivid: the same 78 replies support three population statements. Pooled across respondents, 29.5 per cent said yes. Weighted to the 214 accounts, the expected count of willing accounts is 52.8, or 24.67 per cent. Weighted to revenue — what an 18 per cent uplift actually multiplies — the willing accounts hold ₹23.90 crore of the ₹60.60 crore book, or 39.44 per cent.

None is wrong; each answers a different question. The 18 per cent uplift on ₹23.90 crore is ₹4.30 crore a year, clearing the ₹3.60 crore cost. Priced instead as a flat ₹6 lakh per plant group, the same survey predicts 52.8 × ₹6 lakh = ₹3.17 crore, failing by ₹0.43 crore. Pricing structure decides which weighting is relevant, so the estimand cannot be fixed before pricing is posed — a sequencing point organisations get backwards.

The idea actively misleads twice over. When the purpose is to discover a mechanism rather than measure a magnitude, a representative sample is wasteful: the median customer has nothing unusual to teach. And when the population can be enumerated, sampling theory is an obstacle; at 214 accounts, Ekaagra's better move is the census.

5. Hard edge cases

Two-sided and platform. Chashma's home service needs optometrists as much as customers, and a sample of one side says nothing about the other. Worse, a frame of contracted optometrists excludes exactly those who would join if the service existed, making supply-side sampling partly counterfactual. Mature marketplaces sample the matched pair — the completed visit — and accept that the frame exists only after launch, which is why they run geographic pilots instead of surveys.

Regulated. The invitation needed a lawful basis under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and the consent language narrows the frame: customers who declined marketing contact are unreachable, are plausibly the most privacy-sensitive, and are therefore plausibly the least willing to admit an optometrist into the house. That exclusion correlates with the answer and cannot be weighted away.

Hardware plus software. A survey can be re-fielded cheaply; an order for refraction kits cannot be re-placed. Hardware pushes teams toward larger samples ahead of commitment, so sample size ends up set by irreversibility rather than by any statistical rule.

AI-native. Ekaagra's module trains on sensor histories from whichever plants had instrumented machines — about a quarter of the installed base, heavily weighted to large accounts. That training set is a convenience sample of the population the model will serve, and the bias is self-reinforcing: the module performs best where data was plentiful, so adopters generate more data, so the next model skews further. No weighting fixes a feedback loop; only instrumenting under-represented plants does.

At the organisational seams. Research owns the draw, marketing the invitation, finance the hurdle rate — so nobody owns the estimand. Chashma's memo travelled from Kochi to Jaipur with the response rate in a footnote, which is how 7.35 per cent came to sit below a confident headline. Mature firms fix this not with statistics but with a standing rule that every population claim carries its denominator and response rate, so that stripping them is visibly an omission.

6. Nine distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The estimand precedes everything. The tell: nobody can finish "we are estimating the proportion of ___ that ___". The obvious reading — a sample is good or bad in itself — is wrong: the same 78 Ekaagra replies were excellent for revenue and mediocre for account count.

Response rate is a symptom, not the disease. Bias is governed by the covariance between responding and the answer, not by the share who responded. The tell: relaxing at "36 per cent" and panicking at "7 per cent" without asking what differs between the groups. Xiao-Li Meng's formalisation is brutal — effective sample size falls to roughly n / (1 + (N − n)ρ²), where ρ is that correlation. For Chashma, ρ = 0.05 gives 2,058 / (1 + 11,17,942 × 0.0025) = 0.74: two thousand interviews holding less information than one random customer.

Weighting is a purchase, not a repair. It buys bias reduction with variance at a price the design effect states. The tell: a weighted number quoted with an unweighted margin, as Chashma's first draft did at ±1.90 instead of ±2.10 points.

Weights can only use what the frame holds. Frames hold billing attributes — tier, revenue, tenure — never attitudes. The tell: a deck calling the sample "representative" after weighting on demographics alone, when the driver was something unobserved, such as a prior bad eye test.

Coverage error is invisible and uncorrectable. Non-response leaves a trace in unreturned invitations; a customer never on the frame leaves none, and the sample looks immaculate. The tell: a frame called "all our customers" and never reconciled against the revenue ledger.

Quotas are not strata. Filling a Tier-3 quota of 336 by letting eager Tier-3 customers answer until the box is full yields the right mix and the same within-cell self-selection. The tell: a vendor reporting perfect demographic balance and no response rate. Balance achieved by closing cells is evidence of nothing.

The within-cell assumption holds the residual risk. Post-stratification assumes silent customers resemble talkative ones inside each tier. The tell: an estimate with no sensitivity to that assumption. Section 12 does it honestly, and the result dwarfs the sampling interval.

Intent-to-behaviour ratios are themselves estimates. Chashma's 0.30 came from three launches — a sample of size three, whose uncertainty exceeds the survey's and is almost never carried through. The tell: a conversion factor quoted to two decimals with no range.

In small populations the arithmetic runs the other way. At 78 of 214, the finite-population correction √((214 − 78) / 213) = 0.799 narrows Ekaagra's margin from ±10.12 to ±8.09 percentage points. The tell: a B2B team applying consumer-scale sample-size rules to a population it could simply finish counting.

7. How this differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the frame is large and cheap, so the binding constraint is response, and the craft lies in getting the uninterested to answer. In B2B and enterprise the frame is small and known, so the craft shifts to the unit of analysis and whose voice was captured: Ekaagra heard plant managers, while the signature on an 18 per cent uplift belongs to a group finance head. In platforms two frames interact, so the sample must be of transactions rather than either side. In hardware the decision is irreversible and sample size follows commitment cost, not convention. In AI products the question moves upstream into training and evaluation sets, where the risk is a feedback loop no weighting can undo.

By stage the difference is real but smaller than claimed. An early-stage company lacks a frame worth drawing from and should sample purposively and say so. A scaling company acquires a frame and over-trusts it, because the frame tracks its own acquisition channels rather than the market. A mature company stratifies, weights and keeps a panel, whose characteristic failure is drift. What never changes is naming the estimand, which costs one sentence.

8. Three worked examples

The February failure, and the recovery

Chashma's first attempt, in February 2026, was a store-intercept study: interviewers at nine stores, all in Tier-1 city malls, on weekends. Of 540 intercepts, 216 said they would definitely buy a ₹2,499 version — 40.0 per cent. The 0.30 calibration gave a predicted purchase rate of 12.0 per cent. The pilot ran in 40 stores from 14 March to 25 April 2026, six weeks exactly, and sold the bundle to 1,344 of 22,400 eye-test customers: 6.0 per cent, half the prediction. The diagnosis was coverage, not selection: weekend mall footfall in a Tier-1 city is close to the most enthusiastic quintile of the base, and random selection inside that frame never reaches the rest. The recovery was to rebuild the study on the transacting-customer frame with tier strata, which is Table 1 — and note what that did not deliver: the September study is better and still cannot resolve the decision.

The pricing structure that flipped the answer

Ekaagra's is the cleaner lesson, because nothing about its fieldwork was poor. Response was 36.4 per cent, skewed toward large accounts, and that skew was helpful for a revenue-denominated estimand and harmful for a count-denominated one. The 18 per cent uplift produces ₹4.30 crore against ₹3.60 crore of cost; a flat ₹6 lakh per group produces ₹3.17 crore and fails. Two teams reading the same table reached opposite recommendations in September, and neither made an arithmetic error.

Panel drift, compounded

Chashma also bought a syndicated eyewear panel of 4,000 households in March 2025, with monthly attrition of 2.5 per cent. When Kulgod audited it in September 2026, eighteen months later, the retained original cohort was 0.97518 = 63.4 per cent, or 2,536 of the original 4,000 households, and the vendor's replacements came from the easiest-to-reach cities. The additive reading — 2.5 × 18 = 45 per cent lost — is wrong and comforting in the wrong direction: the true cumulative loss is 36.6 per cent, concentrated among the households hardest to replace like for like.

9. Failure modes, with early warnings

Reading the pooled percentage as the population. Early sign: a headline with no denominator and no response rate. Diagnostic: what is the response rate by a segment on the frame? Cost of catching it late: Chashma's February pilot, six weeks of 40 stores against a forecast twice the truth.

The unstated estimand. Early sign: two teams quoting different percentages from one survey without noticing. Diagnostic: what is the denominator, and does the pricing model multiply it? Cost: a module priced one way and justified by an estimate built the other way.

Treating a panel as a fixed population. Early sign: no attrition figure in the vendor report. Diagnostic: what share of the founding cohort remains? Cost: drift in a tracker read as a change in the market.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does the response rate matter? The sceptical position, supported by a long series of Pew Research Center methodological studies, is that response rates correlate weakly with bias across many estimates, because the hard-to-reach are not systematically different on most questions; on that evidence a 7.35 per cent sample with good covariates is usable. The opposing position, from Robert Groves's non-response literature and Meng's data-defect work, is that a weak average correlation is cold comfort for the one estimate you care about — the one where interest in the product and willingness to answer a survey about it share a cause. For the sceptics to be wrong, response propensity would have to correlate with outcomes far more often than published comparisons show; for the worriers to be wrong here, wanting a home eye test would have to be unrelated to answering a prompt about eye tests.

Probability samples, or large non-probability samples with modelling? The AAPOR task force of 2013 and the comparison studies of David Yeager and colleagues found probability samples more accurate on average than opt-in panels. Against that, Wei Wang, Andrew Gelman and co-authors recovered an accurate 2012 United States election forecast from an Xbox gaming panel using multilevel regression and post-stratification: a severely skewed sample with strong covariates and a good model can beat a mediocre probability sample. The model-based case needs the variables driving selection to be observed; the design-based case needs probability samples to still earn the name.

How much to adjust. One camp calibrates to everything available and accepts large weights; another trims weights to cap variance and accepts residual bias. Kish's design effect prices the choice without resolving it: the bias removed is unobservable while the variance added is measured, an asymmetry that pushes practitioners toward under-adjusting.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently before fieldwork, not after. They write the estimand and the decision threshold on one line before the questionnaire exists, so the break-even figure of 27.86 per cent is known in advance and the survey is designed to discriminate around it. They allocate sample where uncertainty is expensive, over-sampling Tier 3 rather than proportionally. They watch response by stratum from day one, quote a weighted estimate with its effective sample size, and name the assumption the conclusion rests on, so the argument moves to the assumption rather than the number.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Suryavanshi did not take 31.63 per cent to her board on 1 October. She took 26.35 per cent, an interval of 24.25 to 28.45, and the observation that the break-even share of 27.86 per cent lay inside it. Then came the calculation that changed the conversation. If silent customers within each tier are λ percentage points less interested than those who answered, the weighted estimate falls by λ × (0.30 × 0.875 + 0.40 × 0.94 + 0.30 × 0.96) = 0.9265 λ. At λ = 6 the estimate is 20.79 per cent; at λ = −6 it is 31.91 per cent. That band is 11.12 points wide, more than two and a half times the 4.20-point sampling interval, and break-even requires λ = −1.63: the silent must be more interested than the vocal. She recommended against launch and proposed a paid eight-city test at ₹1,799 with over-sampled Tier-3 cities, which the board approved.

Raghavendra decided on 6 October to build, but his reasoning concerned the denominator, not the data. He fixed the estimand as revenue addressed, kept the 18 per cent uplift that made revenue the right denominator, and committed to a census of the remaining 136 accounts before contracting, since at 214 accounts enumeration costs weeks rather than statistics. He also recorded what his survey could not tell him: plant managers had answered, and group finance would sign.

Three questions. First, Chashma's break-even requires that silent customers be 1.63 points more interested than vocal ones; what evidence, obtainable before launch, would make that credible or absurd? Second, if Ekaagra finishes its census and 136 more accounts answer, which of the three estimates in Figure 1 can still be wrong, and why? Third, the 0.30 intent-to-purchase ratio rests on three observations; would you spend the next ₹10 lakh on a larger survey or on sharpening that ratio?

13. Going deeper

  • Survey design — wording fixes what the answer means before sampling arises.
  • Weighting and non-response correction — formalises Table 1, adding raking and propensity models.
  • Consumer panels and syndicated data — someone else chose your sample; drift becomes your problem.
  • Descriptive statistics for PMs — the standard errors and intervals this page assumes.
  • Quantitative concept testing — stated intent into a calibrated forecast, as the 0.30 ratio does.
  • Conjoint and MaxDiff — designs that curb intent overstatement but demand more sample.
  • Statistical segmentation — how strata get chosen, and why choosing them from the same data is circular.
  • NPS, CSAT and CES — trackers whose movement is often a change in who responded.
  • The Sean Ellis PMF survey — a benchmark resting on no probability sample.

Kasturi Naturals: Who Answered the Sachet Question?

A ₹ 148 crore launch rests on a purchase-intent number that three studies cannot agree on. One of them reached the people the product is for.

1. The night before

At twenty to midnight on Sunday 11 October 2026, Elakshi Tungare was alone on the eighth floor of Kasturi Naturals' office in Prabhadevi, Mumbai, the board pack open in one window and a spreadsheet she had shown nobody in the other. At 9.30 the next morning the pack would ask for ₹ 148 crore — ₹ 86 crore of capex, ₹ 62 crore of first-year advertising — to launch an eight-millilitre face-serum sachet at ₹ 10 into towns the company had never sold into properly.

Slide 9 was the problem. It carried one number in 96-point type: 63.5 per cent, under the words National purchase intent, top-two-box. Three things it did not say: it was unweighted; it described an online panel whose members disproportionately owned a smartphone and used a cashback app; and its footnote gave the base as n = 3,744, the number who finished the questionnaire, when the 63.5 per cent was computed on the 3,320 whose answers survived exclusion.

Two other studies sat beneath the pack. A September face-to-face survey in eight small towns put intent at 44.0 per cent. A twelve-week shelf pilot in six towns reported a 27.0 per cent repeat rate, which sales quoted as buyer repeat and which was the share of people who had scanned a cashback QR code twice; nobody knew how many had bought a sachet at all. Ekagra Tawde, the co-founder and chief executive, had said on Friday that the sachet was the company's third act and the board had been told it was coming. Elakshi typed a line — what would have to be true for 63.5 and 44.0 to both be right? — and deleted it, suspecting that both could be, and that this was the problem.

2. The company, and one decision from 2024

Kasturi Naturals was founded in Pune in 2019 selling a cold-pressed hair oil through Instagram. Its hero product since 2022 has been a 30 ml face serum at ₹ 349, and its growth followed the shape familiar to its cohort: Amazon and Flipkart listings, a Nykaa shelf, then a violent re-platforming onto quick commerce as Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart rewrote urban buying. Revenue reached ₹ 980 crore in FY26 (Exhibit 5).

Two earlier decisions constrain tonight. In November 2024, to get general-trade distribution without building a field force, Kasturi signed a three-year exclusive arrangement with a super-stockist network across eleven states, expiring 31 October 2027. A clause negotiated when nothing sold below ₹ 199 fixes the super-stockist margin on any unit under ₹ 50 at 9.5 per cent, so the sachet plan passes through a contract written for something else.

The second shaped the evidence. In April 2024 Eshwari Tatachar, newly hired to head consumer insights, pre-paid ₹ 4.2 crore for two years of unlimited online fieldwork with Kritti Panel Services, later extended to March 2027. It made research feel free at the margin: for two and a half years the cheapest way to ask Indian consumers anything was to ask Kritti's panel — and nobody wrote down what that panel was a sample of.

3. The industry

In Indian beauty and personal care the sachet is the standard technology of trial: Hindustan Unilever built a rural shampoo business on ₹ 1 sachets, and Cavinkare's Chik is taught in every Indian marketing classroom. At a ₹ 349 entry price a household earning ₹ 22,000 a month will not take a trial risk; a ₹ 10 unit turns the decision into an impulse. The premium set — Mamaearth, Minimalist, Plum — is not where that fight is.

Three forces complicate the copy-paste. Channel: quick commerce is 41 per cent of revenue and dark stores do not stock ₹ 10 units, so the sachet is a general-trade and ONDC product while the company's demand data comes from channels where it will not exist. Regulation: Legal Metrology unit-price disclosure puts the per-millilitre premium on pack, the DPDP Act has tightened what a cashback-linked QR programme may collect, and cosmetic claims sit with the CDSCO. Exposure abroad: 7.9 per cent of FY26 revenue came from Gulf Cooperation Council markets through one Dubai distributor, Kahraman General Trading, whose contract carries a ₹ 11 crore half-yearly minimum order value and a most-favoured-pricing clause a ₹ 10 India sachet would arguably trip.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The sachet was formalised in February 2026, and the universe written down: women and men aged 18–45 in households earning ₹ 15,000 to ₹ 75,000 a month who bought any face-care product in the previous three months — an estimated 24.0 crore people, from Census projections and household consumption tabulations. Nobody has disputed it since.

Study A was fielded on Kritti's panel between 18 May and 9 June 2026. Exhibit 1 gives the funnel; the point is that it passed through seven different bases on the way to a percentage, and the deck quotes the last of them wrongly. Kritti's ninety-day-active panel numbered 2,86,000 — one member per 839 people in the universe. The response rate, completes over invited, was 7.8 per cent; the 24.0 per cent in the table is the screener-start rate, a different quantity. Of 3,744 completes, 3,320 survived exclusion, and every published Study A figure is computed on 3,320.

In July the deck went to the board with 63.5 per cent. Three weeks later an investor asked how many people in the sample lived in the towns where the sachet would be sold: 599, or 18.0 per cent of the analysable sample, against 48.0 per cent of the universe. Eshwari commissioned a face-to-face booster that week. Emmeline Toussaint, in Toronto, had built the post-stratification in Exhibit 2, which pulls intent to 59.0 per cent and widens the interval to ±2.2 points. Her memo of 28 September said post-stratification cannot repair a frame: it only makes the people who are in the sample stand in for those who are not, and in the Tier 3-and-rural cells each respondent stood for roughly 1.9 lakh people. Study B (Exhibit 3), run by Kosha Field Research from 1 to 23 September, achieved 912 of a 1,200 target and returned pooled intent of 44.0 per cent at ±4.1 points. The intervals do not touch: 56.8 to 61.2 against 39.9 to 48.1.

Two things have since turned out not to be what was believed. On 6 October Kritti disclosed that its March 2026 refresh had recruited 61 per cent of its Tier 3-and-below members through one cashback application, and that those members were 38,900 of the 2,86,000 active panel — 13.6 per cent of the frame against 48.0 per cent of the universe. The same mail noted duplicate detection was switched on only in July, so Study A's 48 removed duplicates came from a retrospective pass the vendor rates at about 70 per cent sensitivity. And on 2 October Ekansh Thorat's team in Pune established that the pilot's 27.0 per cent repeat rate is a rate among scanners, not buyers (Exhibit 4).

5. The people

Elakshi owns the recommendation; her bonus rides on the sachet's first-year gross contribution, and she has not told Ekagra she thinks 63.5 per cent should be struck from the deck she approved in July. Seven others, plus Emaan Topiwala, category head at the Dubai distributor — who wants a carve-out in writing and is not saying that two rival Indian brands have approached him with similar plans — each have a position, an incentive and something unsaid.

Ekagra Tawde — Co-founder and Chief Executive, Mumbai

Jamakhata: The Survey That Only Some Merchants Answered

A decision case on sampling and representativeness

1. Opening

On the morning of Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Devika Salunkhe, chief product officer of Jamakhata, sat in a glass meeting room on the fourth floor of the company's office in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, with a single slide on her screen. It carried one number: 61.5 per cent. That was the share of merchants who had answered "yes" in an in-app survey when asked whether they would pay ₹299 a month for a new inventory-credit plan. Her chief executive wanted the product council to approve a ₹3.6 crore build and launch budget on Thursday, 22 October, so that the plan could reach shopkeepers before the Diwali fortnight in early November, the weeks in which kirana owners stock up hardest.

Devika did not doubt the arithmetic. She doubted what the number was a number of. Only a small fraction of the merchants invited had answered, the people who answered were not spread across the country the way the customer base was, and a majority of registered merchants had never been in a position to receive the survey at all. She had eight days to decide whether to take the number to the council as it stood, as a corrected number, or not at all.

2. Company background

Jamakhata, founded in 2019 by two former payments engineers, sells a free digital ledger and a UPI collection tool to small retailers: kirana stores, chemists, tea stalls and the like. It earns from payment-linked fees and from a few paid add-ons. By October 2026 it had 12,00,000 registered merchants. Of these, 4,80,000 had opened the app at least once in the previous thirty days; the company calls them its active merchants. The other 7,20,000 had registered, often at the urging of a field agent, and drifted away.

The competitive field is crowded. Khatabook and OkCredit own the ledger habit, Paytm and PhonePe for Business own the soundbox and the QR code, and Zoho Books and Vyapar compete for merchants who need invoices. Reliance Retail's JioMart Partner and the ONDC network are pulling distributors toward credit offers of their own, and every lending product must now comply with the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending guidelines, which is why Jamakhata's plan would be delivered through a regulated lending partner. The company's earlier add-on, a printed-receipt feature, had converted roughly 15 per cent of the merchants who said they would buy it, and the product team has used that figure as a working assumption for the new plan, though it has not been measured for credit.

3. The situation

The survey was Devika's own request. In September her team drew 60,000 merchants at random from the 4,80,000 active frame, 12.5 per cent of it, and sent each an in-app prompt and a WhatsApp reminder. Of the 60,000 invited, 5,100 started the questionnaire and 4,200 completed it: a response rate of 7.0 per cent, computed as completes over invited. Exhibit 1 sets out each stage and the base it is measured on, and Exhibit 2 gives the picture by city tier.

Two facts stand out. First, the frame excludes 60.0 per cent of registered merchants, so every statement from the survey is at best a statement about active merchants. Second, the response rate is far from uniform. Metro merchants completed at 10.8 per cent of those invited, tier-2 merchants at 5.3 per cent and tier-3 and smaller-town merchants at 5.1 per cent. Metro merchants are only 32.5 per cent of the active frame but 50.0 per cent of the completes.

The "yes" rate falls steeply with city size: 71.0 per cent in metros, 60.0 per cent in tier 2, 40.0 per cent in tier 3 and smaller. The headline 61.5 per cent is therefore the average of a sample that over-represents the most enthusiastic tier. Re-weighting the cells to their true shares of the active frame gives 58.1 per cent. Because the weights are not extreme, the design effect is small: with the Kish formula and weights scaled to mean 1, the sum of n × w² is 4,715.375 against 4,200 completes, so the design effect is 4,715.375 / 4,200 = 1.1227 and the effective sample is 4,200 / 1.1227 = 3,741. At 95 per cent confidence, simple random sampling within cells and a normal approximation, the margin of error on 58.1 per cent, computed on the effective n of 3,741, is about ±1.6 points; the unweighted 61.5 per cent on the nominal n = 4,200 carries ±1.5 points. Both margins are tight, and both are misleading in the same way: they measure only the noise from drawing 4,200 respondents, and say nothing about the 55,800 invited merchants who did not complete, or the 7,20,000 who were never asked.

The global team reads the numbers from where they sit. Darshan Seth, the data scientist in Toronto, built Exhibit 2 and has warned that weighting repairs the tier mix but cannot repair a bias inside a tier: a tier-3 shopkeeper who answers an in-app survey in English or Hindi is probably more digitally confident than the tier-3 shopkeeper who does not. Delphine Soo, the customer-success lead in Singapore, telephoned 40 tier-3 merchants herself and heard 14 say yes, 35 per cent. That is an anecdote, not a sample: on 40 calls the margin is roughly ±15 points, so 35 per cent is consistent with the survey's 40 per cent and also with something much lower. In Pune, Dnyanesh Sapre, who leads engineering, needs a go decision by the end of October to hold his team's Diwali-week slot. Dagny Schreiber, the product designer in Berlin, has pointed out that the survey was written in English and Hindi only, which may itself have sorted respondents.

One more consideration: collecting survey responses and phone numbers for follow-up falls under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, so any further contact needs consent captured in advance and cannot simply reuse the September list.

4. The people

Devika Salunkhe (Bengaluru, chief product officer) must carry a recommendation to the council on 22 October. She wants a decision she can defend if the plan succeeds and, more importantly, if it does not. Dnyanesh Sapre (Pune, head of engineering) wants certainty about the slot, since a slipped start means his team is redeployed for a quarter. Darshan Seth (Toronto, data scientist) wants the council to hear a range and its assumptions rather than a single figure. Delphine Soo (Singapore, customer success) wants the plan to reach the small-town merchants she calls every week, and worries that the survey describes a different Jamakhata from the one they use. Dagny Schreiber (Berlin, design) wants to know whether the people who did not answer would have understood the question.

5. Exhibits and the economics

The plan pays back only if enough merchants subscribe. Finance estimates that each subscriber contributes ₹1,000 a year after lending-partner costs, so the ₹3.6 crore budget is recovered in year one at 36,000 subscribers. That is 7.5 per cent of the 4,80,000 active merchants. If 15 per cent of merchants who say "yes" subscribe, as the receipt feature suggests, break-even needs 36,000 / 0.15 = 2,40,000 stated "yes" merchants, that is 50.0 per cent of the active frame. Exhibit 3 shows how much room each reading of the survey leaves.

Read at face value the weighted result clears break-even by 5,814 subscribers, a margin of about 16 per cent. But a modest drop in the true conversion rate, or a modest overstatement of interest by those who chose to respond, erases it. If the conversion rate is 12.5 per cent rather than 15, the weighted result gives 2,78,760 × 0.125 = 34,845 subscribers, which falls short.

6. The options

Option A: approve now on the weighted number. Take 58.1 per cent to the council, commit the full ₹3.6 crore on 22 October and launch before Diwali. Upside: the festival season and the Pune slot are both kept, and the competitors' credit offers do not get a clear run. Cost: the entire budget is committed on a figure that speaks only for active, responding merchants, with a thin margin over break-even and no evidence on the 60.0 per cent of the base outside the frame.

Option B: commission a probability survey first. Spend ₹18 lakh on a phone and field survey of 1,500 merchants, a stratified random sample drawn from all 12,00,000 registered with fixed allocations by tier (no quotas filled by whoever picks up), and calls in the local language. Upside: it covers the dormant base and reduces self-selection; the margin of error on a proportion near 50 per cent at n = 1,500 is ±2.5 points (1.96 × √(0.25 / 1,500) = 2.53). That figure assumes simple random sampling and a full response from everyone drawn; phone response among dormant merchants will be low, so non-response bias, the very problem this case teaches, would remain and the true uncertainty is wider. Cost: the results arrive at the end of November, after Diwali, the engineering slot is lost, and the survey still measures stated intent rather than behaviour.

Option C: release a staged pilot. Release ₹55 lakh of the budget to launch the plan to a random 20,000 of the 4,80,000 active merchants, selected within tier in proportion to the frame (all invited merchants are offered the plan, so no one is selected for being enthusiastic). Read take-up on 8 December against the 7.5 per cent threshold, which is an annual-equivalent simplification: it is the year-one break-even of 36,000 subscribers over the whole frame, whereas the pilot sees only a few weeks of take-up after a launch that cannot precede the 22 October council, and the ₹1,000 contribution is per subscriber-year, so early take-up may under- or overstate year-one subscribers. At 7.5 per cent and n = 20,000 the 95 per cent sampling margin is ±0.37 points (1.96 × √(0.075 × 0.925 / 20,000)), which measures sampling noise only. Upside: it measures behaviour, not intention, on a representative draw from the frame, and the engineering slot is kept. Cost: it delays full rollout past Diwali, still covers only active merchants, and the remaining ₹3.05 crore is held back.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Name the target population, the frame and the achieved sample in this case. Which merchants are in the population but not in the frame, and what does that do to the claim "61.5 per cent of Jamakhata merchants would pay"?

2. Using Exhibit 2, explain how the relative weights were produced and show that they reconcile to the frame. Why does weighting move the estimate from 61.5 to 58.1 per cent, and what bias can it not correct?

3. Both margins of error are about ±1.5 points. Why should the council not treat that as the real uncertainty? How would the response rates by tier change your answer?

4. Compare the three options on what each can claim, which merchants it covers, how much it costs in rupees and in time, and what Devika should tell the council on 22 October.

8. A note for the learner

The topic frames the decision as a question about who answered. A sample is never "the market"; it is a draw from a frame, shaped by who was invited and who chose to reply. The first discipline is to name every base: registered (12,00,000), frame (4,80,000), invited (60,000), completed (4,200). The second is to ask where the silence is. Here it is in two places: 93.0 per cent of the invited did not complete, and 60.0 per cent of the registered base was never in the frame. Weighting by tier is a sound, cheap correction for the first problem only to the extent that responders resemble non-responders within each tier, and it does nothing for the second.

A well-reasoned answer therefore does three things. It restates the claim at its true scope: roughly 58 per cent of responding, active merchants, weighted by tier, said they would pay. It converts the claim into the quantity that matters, subscribers, using an assumption and shows how fragile break-even is to that assumption (Exhibit 3). And it matches the cost of being wrong to the cost of learning more.

One defensible path: Option C. The survey cannot be the final word and a second survey would still only measure intent, late. The pilot is a random sample from the frame that measures what the council cares about, paid subscriptions, and its sampling precision (±0.37 points, noise only) is far finer than any survey of this budget could give, though the 7.5 per cent bar is a guide to be adjusted for the short window, not a mechanical go/no-go rule. It spends ₹55 lakh instead of ₹3.6 crore before the doubt is resolved, and keeps Dnyanesh's team working through Diwali. Devika should tell the council plainly that the result will apply to active merchants only, that tier-3 take-up should be reported separately because that is where the survey's 40.0 per cent suggests the plan could fail, and that a small consented phone follow-up with non-responders, in local languages, would be a cheap partial check on non-response. Option B is a reasonable alternative if the council puts a high value on the dormant base; Option A is defensible only if the council accepts that it is buying the plan on a stated-interest figure with a margin of 16 per cent over break-even.

Sampling and representativeness

Who answered, who did not, and what that does to the conclusion

1. The survey that said yes

On 2 September 2026, Sunaina Hosmani, head of product at Hamsafar Bus Exchange, opened a one-page summary from her analyst, Himanshi Tandon, working from the company's Hubballi office. Hamsafar sells intercity bus tickets through an app and a website, and counts 4,00,000 monthly active users. The summary concerned a proposed product called Seat Assurance: a monthly subscription at ₹49 that promised a full refund, or a seat on the next departure, if a booked bus was cancelled or ran badly late. Building it would cost, in engineering time, partner guarantees and expected refunds, about ₹55 lakh every month. The subscription had to earn more than that or it should not be built.

The survey had run from 24 to 30 August. An in-app banner had asked 20,000 randomly chosen users whether they would subscribe at ₹49. The headline was encouraging: 988 of the 2,860 users who answered said yes, a share of 34.5 per cent. Applied to 4,00,000 users, that implied roughly 1,38,000 subscribers and about ₹67.7 lakh a month, comfortably above the ₹55 lakh hurdle. Sudhir Kamat, the finance lead, had pencilled the launch into the October plan.

Hosmani hesitated over a different number on the same page: only 14.3 per cent of invited users had answered. The steering committee met on 9 September. If she endorsed the headline and it was wrong, Hamsafar would commit a year of engineering effort and guarantee contracts with bus operators to a product that lost money every month. If she rejected it and it was right, a rival such as redBus could take the idea first. Her question was narrow: who answered, who did not, and what does that do to what the result means?

2. The idea

A population is the whole group a decision is about; here, the 4,00,000 monthly active users. A sample is the part of it actually observed. A sample is representative when the part resembles the whole in every respect that bears on the question being asked. No sample resembles its population in every respect; it need only do so in the respects that move the answer.

Sampling solves a practical problem: observing everyone is slow, costly and sometimes impossible. The modern machinery came from the early twentieth century. Statisticians such as Jerzy Neyman showed in the 1930s that a small random sample could describe a large population with a quantifiable error, and that purposive selection by an expert, however thoughtful, could not offer that guarantee. The Literary Digest poll of 1936 supplied the cautionary tale: millions of replies, a confident forecast, and the wrong president, because those who replied were not the electorate. In India, the National Sample Survey, begun in 1950 under P. C. Mahalanobis, made sampling a working discipline.

The sentence Hosmani could repeat in a meeting: "The sample tells us what the people who answered think; our job is to show whether they look like the people we are deciding about."

3. How it actually works

Three separate steps stand between a population and a conclusion, and practitioners often blur them into one. First comes coverage: the list from which people can be drawn, called the sampling frame. Hamsafar's frame was its list of active app users, which already excludes anyone who books by phone through an agent. Second comes selection: how names are drawn from the frame. A simple random sample gives every name an equal chance; a stratified sample first splits the frame into groups, called strata, and draws randomly within each. Third comes response: which of those drawn actually answer. Non-response bias is the distortion that arises when the people who answer differ from those who do not, in a way connected to the question.

The third step is the one outside the researcher's control, and the one usually left implicit. Hamsafar's draw was clean: 20,000 users chosen at random, which means each segment appeared in proportion to its share of the user base. Hosmani asked Tandon to split users by travel frequency, which plausibly drove both the chance of answering a banner and the value of an assurance product (Table 1).

The skew matters only if the segments think differently about the product, and they did. Had they not, over-representing heavy users would be harmless: being unrepresentative on a variable is a problem only when that variable is related to the answer.

4. A worked example

Tandon's raw figure pooled all respondents. Table 2 separates them. Interest among respondents was 60 per cent for heavy users, 30 per cent for medium and 10 per cent for light users. The pooled figure is 988 / 2,860 = 34.5 per cent. That is the figure on the page Hosmani received.

Weighting repairs the mix. Each heavy respondent stands for 60,000 / 900 = 66.7 users, each medium respondent for 1,40,000 / 1,260 = 111.1, each light respondent for 2,00,000 / 700 = 285.7. The weighted share is 24.5 per cent, not 34.5. At ₹49 a month, 98,000 subscribers yield ₹48,02,000, or ₹48.02 lakh. The unweighted figure would have implied 34.545 per cent of 4,00,000, which is about 1,38,182 subscribers and ₹67.71 lakh. The first falls short of the ₹55 lakh monthly cost; the second clears it. The entire disagreement is a matter of who happened to answer a banner.

A weighted figure has uncertainty too. Combining the three segment errors in proportion to their weights, the 95 per cent margin is about 1.5 percentage points, so the weighted share runs from 23.0 to 26.0 per cent, or 92,000 to 1,04,000 subscribers. The break-even is ₹55,00,000 / ₹49 = about 1,12,245 subscribers, which is 28.1 per cent of users. Even the top of the range sits below it.

Second pass. Weighting assumes that, within a segment, those who did not answer resemble those who did. Suppose that is false for light users: those who ignored the banner are somewhat more interested than those who answered, giving a true light-user interest of 14 per cent instead of 10. The weighted share becomes 0.15 × 60 + 0.35 × 30 + 0.50 × 14 = 9.0 + 10.5 + 7.0 = 26.5 per cent, or 1,06,000 subscribers and ₹51.94 lakh a month. Still short of ₹55 lakh. For the product to break even, light-user interest would have to reach about 17.1 per cent, since 9.0 + 10.5 + 0.5 × 17 = 28.0. Hosmani now knew which assumption to defend.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Size does not cure bias

The error from an unrepresentative mix is not reduced by adding more of the same respondents; it is merely measured more precisely around the wrong value. The Literary Digest failure was exactly this.

Random selection and representative response are different things

Hamsafar's draw was random; the respondents were self-selected. Randomness protects only the first step.

Representative on what?

There is no representative sample in the abstract. Hamsafar's was badly off on travel frequency, which mattered, and perhaps fine on age or city. Name the variable first.

Weighting corrects what you can see, not what you cannot

Weighting by frequency works because frequency is known for every user in the frame. It cannot repair a difference between answerers and non-answerers inside a segment, which is what the second pass probed. That residue is the edge of what the method can tell you.

Stated intent is not behaviour

Even a perfect sample reports what people say they would do, and respondents routinely overstate intent. The 24.5 per cent is a ceiling on stated interest, not a forecast of subscriptions.

Questions to ask before relying on it

Who was in the frame, and who was not? How many answered, in which groups? What would change the decision?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products; early and late stage

In consumer products, the frame is huge and cheap, so the danger is the self-selecting banner, as at Hamsafar. In B2B, the population may be a few hundred accounts, and sampling means something different: when a company has 120 customers, a survey that reaches 30 of them is a quarter of the population, and the issue is less random error than which stakeholder, buyer or user, answered. A handful of large accounts may supply most revenue and must be weighted by value, not head count.

In a marketplace there are two populations, and a sample of one side says nothing about the other. Hamsafar's bus operators, who would have to honour the guarantee, were not surveyed at all, though their willingness mattered as much as riders' interest.

By stage, an early-stage company often has too few users for random draws to be meaningful, and sensibly relies on twenty conversations chosen on purpose. That deliberate, non-random sample suits finding out what people think, not how many think it. A large company has the data to stratify and weight; its risk is a standing panel that drifts as members age and drop out.

7. Common mistakes

Reading the headline percentage as the population

Symptom: a result is quoted with no mention of response rate or composition. Misunderstanding: assuming answers are a miniature of the user base. Diagnostic: ask for the response rate by known segment; five minutes with a table like Table 1.

Treating a large n as proof

Symptom: "we had thousands of responses" offered as the defence. Misunderstanding: confusing precision with accuracy. Diagnostic: ask what the answer would be if only the most eager 10 per cent had replied; compare to the full set.

Weighting on variables that do not matter

Symptom: elaborate adjustments by age and city that barely move the number. Misunderstanding: weighting everything available. Diagnostic: check whether the answer differs across the variable at all; if not, leave it alone.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the work begins before fieldwork. Hosmani would have named frequency as the variable likely to drive both response and interest, and stratified the draw to oversample light users, since they were half the base and the hardest to hear from. She would have sent a reminder in week two and tracked response by segment from day one. The summary would state the frame, the draw, response by segment, the pooled figure, the weighted figure with its margin, and the one assumption, that silent users resemble talkative ones within a segment, on which the answer rests. The note would also say what consent the invitation relied on under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

At the 9 September meeting Hosmani did not present 34.5 per cent. She presented 24.5 per cent with a range of 23.0 to 26.0, showed Table 1, and said that the product, as priced, would not cover its ₹55 lakh monthly cost on stated intent, which is the generous case. She proposed instead a four-week test with real sign-ups among a random 5,000 light and medium users, and talks with six bus operators. The committee agreed. A launch built on 34.5 per cent would be defended by the word "survey"; one built on 24.5 per cent could be defended by the arithmetic.

To go further, study weighting and non-response correction, which formalises what Table 2 did by hand, and consumer panels and syndicated data, where someone else has already chosen the sample.

Two questions to sit with. First, suppose Hamsafar had received a 60 per cent response rate by obliging users to answer before booking; which new biases might that create? Second, which decision at your own organisation currently rests on a number whose response rate you have never seen?
